extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, media professionals, public relations practitioners, and the general public interested in media ethics and broadcast practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for creating, distributing, and assessing Video News Releases (VNRs): what they are, common production practices, ethical concerns, broadcaster selection criteria, and relevant U.S. legal/regulatory constraints. Useful for PR producers, broadcasters, and media-ethics reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Video News Release (VNR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A video segment made to look like a news report, but is instead created by a PR firm, advertising agency, marketing firm, corporation, government agency, or non-profit organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to shape public opinion, promote products/services, publicize individuals, or support other interests. Producers consider VNRs the video-equivalent of a press release; broadcasters may choose whether to air them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure / identification to viewers
rubrics_metrics.description: VNRs that are not identified to the viewers as a VNR have been called deceptive or a propaganda technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory and ethical guidance implies that the origin of the footage should be disclosed; the FCC warned stations they could be fined for airing stories provided by government/companies without disclosing who made them. Avoid presenting VNR content as station-originated reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial discretion / newsworthiness test for broadcasters
rubrics_metrics.description: News producers may air VNRs, in whole or in part, at their discretion or incorporate them into news reports if they contain information appropriate to a story or of interest to viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasters should exercise editorial judgment about whether material is newsworthy and relevant. The decision to use, excerpt, edit, or rewrite scripts remains a newsroom responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of professional reporters, on-air talent, or actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Most VNRs feature a professional news reporter, someone with on-air news experience, or an actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using on-air talent or actors can make a VNR appear like genuine reporting; ethical practice requires clarity about whether persons are acting or are independent journalists. Presenting actors as spontaneous interviewees is misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and treatment of interviews / 'man on the street' segments
rubrics_metrics.description: VNRs often include interviews with experts, 'man on the street' interviews with 'average' people, and other staged comments; sometimes actors are hired and directed to deliver carefully scripted comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers/editors routinely excerpt and edit interviews into 'sound bites' to emphasize a message. Evaluators should watch for scripted or staged segments presented as spontaneous public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and creation of sound bites
rubrics_metrics.description: VNR producers and directors have complete discretion to excerpt and edit interviews into 'sound bites' that help make the point they are trying to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing choices can materially shape meaning and may mislead if context is removed. Assess VNRs for selective editing that alters or oversimplifies source intent or facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial vs. full broadcast practices and script usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial television stations and other media outlets often broadcast only portions of a VNR. Sometimes they use the script provided by the VNR producer but frequently they write their own script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because stations may re-script or re-edit supplied material, they must ensure transparency about source and avoid disguising supplied content as original reporting. Investigations have found stations sometimes actively disguised VNR content to appear as their own reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracking / encoding of VNR materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Public Relations agencies have their video tapes encoded allowing very accurate tracking of where such video is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encoding is a distribution/measurement practice used to monitor placement; it’s a production/placement standard rather than an editorial standard, but signals PR industry practices and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stated purpose / commercial PR objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The VNR placement agency seeks to garner media attention for the client's products, services, brands or other marketing goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating VNRs, consider the client's marketing objectives and how the piece frames issues to support those objectives; treat VNRs primarily as paid/provocative messaging rather than independent journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical concerns: propaganda and manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics have called the practice deceptive or a propaganda technique, particularly when the segment is not identified to the viewers as a VNR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical evaluation should consider whether the piece manipulates public opinion, disguises sponsorship, or undermines editorial independence. Best practice: transparent labeling and avoidance of covert persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government-produced VNRs and legal constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Government agencies (e.g., Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Education, Census Bureau) have produced and distributed VNRs; some such uses were ruled by the GAO to be violations of federal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government-produced VNRs risk breaching statutes and policies (e.g., Smith–Mundt Act concerns and GAO decisions). Public-sector producers must ensure compliance with laws prohibiting covert propaganda and follow procurement/contract rules about promotional material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory oversight and potential penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Communications Commission warned stations they could be fined for airing news stories provided by the government and by companies without disclosing who made them; the FCC has investigated airing of VNRs and sent letters to stations asking about agreements and 'consideration'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasters and VNR distributors should be aware of FCC inquiries, disclosure requirements, and potential enforcement actions; documenting agreements and disclosures reduces legal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented misuse / case examples as evaluation benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific cases have illustrated misuse — e.g., the 'Karen Ryan' video (HHS) ruled in violation by GAO; Dept. of Education VNRs similarly criticized; in May 2020 multiple stations aired a PR piece produced by Amazon with anchors reading identical scripts verbatim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such case studies as cautionary examples when assessing VNR practices: check for undisclosed sponsorship, use of actors as reporters, identical anchor scripts across stations, and government-originated propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry position: PRSA equivalence to press release
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the Public Relations Society of America, a VNR is the video equivalent of a press release and presents a client's case in an attractive, informative format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize VNRs as PR outputs meant to present a client’s viewpoint; evaluate them with the same skepticism applied to press releases regarding bias and intent.
